newsitem.title: FRANCE: Up to 59 die in two-day massacres in Algeria - report.
newsitem.headline: Up to 59 die in two-day massacres in Algeria - report.

text.p: Suspected Moslem rebels killed up to 59 people in raids on hamlets near Algiers in the Moslem Algerian weekend, bringing to more than 250 the number of people killed in Algeria in the past two weeks, an Algerian newspaper said on Saturday.

The news of continuing killings in Algeria's main dailies came hours after President Liamine Zeroual said his government will battle to wipe out guerrillas. He was speaking after a series of massacres and bombings, mostly in Algiers and surrounding towns.

"Fifty-nine have been assassinated during this weekend in the centre of the country, mostly in Berroughia and in douars (villages) of Benramdane, Saouala and Baraki (near Algiers)," said Le Matin quoting villagers.

Guerrillas killed 23 people by cutting their throats on Wednesday in Oumaria in Berrouaghia, 70 km (40 miles) south of Algiers, said Le Matin, without elaborating. These were in addition to the Thursday-Friday killings, it said.
The newspaper, quoting unnamed sources, said the four massacres were carried by rebels from Algeria's ruthless Armed Islamic Group (GIA).

Liberte newspaper, which reported two massacres, said about 50 Moslem guerrillas stormed the small village of Houach el Hadj, some 40 km (25 miles) south of Algiers, and hacked to death 15 villagers about 30 minutes before Friday prayer.
The guerrillas killed 19 people, including 10 women and a two-year-old baby, by using axes and machetes in the neighbouring village of Benramdane, said Liberte.

The GIA had vowed to increase attacks during the Moslem fasting month of Ramadan which began on January 10. They have said Ramadan is the most fit time for their "holy war" against Zeroual's government.
The massacres in villages were in addition to bombings, mostly in Algiers and surrounding towns in the past two weeks.
Zeroual vowed on Friday his country would battle to the "final eradication of terrorism" which he said was being manipulated by foreigners bent on destabilising the North African country.
About 60,000 people have been killed in Algeria's violence since early 1992 when the authorities cancelled a general election in which radical Islamists had taken a commanding lead.
